content: Stockholm syndrome is a psychological phenomenon observed in some hostages who develop emotional bonds and loyalty toward their captors, even when their captors pose a direct threat to their safety. This response has also been noted in other high-stress or abusive situations, such as cases of domestic violence, child abuse, rape, and bride kidnapping. The term originated from the 1973 Norrmalmstorg robbery in Stockholm, Sweden, where bank employees were held hostage for six days. Remarkably, the hostages defended their captors after their release. The term Stockholm syndrome was coined by criminologist and psychiatrist Nils Bejerot, who assisted the police during the incident and later referred to the phenomenon in a news broadcast. Victims of Stockholm syndrome often exhibit loyalty to their abuser, even when provided opportunities to escape or offered safe alternatives, such as foster homes or shelters. This behavior is frequently observed in victims of domestic abuse, battered partners, and dependent children. Psychoanalysts from the object relations theory school have described this as a psychological identification with a more powerful abuser. In some cases, victims continue to justify the abuse they endured, even into adulthood, particularly in situations involving abusive parents or siblings. From an evolutionary psychology perspective, Stockholm syndrome may be linked to survival strategies developed by infants, who form emotional attachments to powerful adults to ensure their survival. This behavior is thought to be an example of the defense mechanism of identification, where the victim aligns psychologically with the abuser to cope with the trauma. Several real-life cases illustrate Stockholm syndrome. For example, Colleen Stan was held captive from 1977 to 1984 by Cameron and Janice Hooker, during which she was subjected to severe physical and sexual abuse. Despite opportunities to escape, she remained with her captors. Her case raised questions about whether she was brainwashed into compliance or willingly participated in her own captivity, as her captor claimed. Another notable case is that of Patty Hearst, a wealthy heiress kidnapped by the Symbionese Liberation Army (SLA) in 1974. After two months in captivity, she participated in a robbery orchestrated by the SLA. Her legal defense argued that she suffered from Stockholm syndrome and was coerced into aiding her captors. However, she was convicted and imprisoned, though her sentence was later commuted by President Jimmy Carter, and she received a presidential pardon from Bill Clinton. Natascha Kampusch, an Austrian teenager kidnapped at age 10 and held captive for eight years, also displayed signs of Stockholm syndrome. After escaping in 2006, she grieved the suicide of her captor, Wolfgang Priklopil. Similarly, Shawn Hornbeck, abducted at age 11 and held for four years, adopted his captor's last name and did not seek help from law enforcement, even when he had the opportunity. His case sparked speculation about whether he suffered from Stockholm syndrome, though many empathized with his decisions. In contrast to Stockholm syndrome, Lima syndrome describes a situation where captors develop sympathy for their hostages. This was observed during the 1996 Japanese embassy hostage crisis in Lima, Peru, where members of the MRTA guerrilla group became more empathetic toward their hostages' needs and well-being.
